bottleneck: Gene therapy trials typically enroll tiny patient populations, run single-arm without controls, and follow patients briefly — designs that generate deep uncertainty about true efficacy and durability. Small samples cannot detect rare serious adverse events, and the lack of comparators makes it hard to separate treatment effects from natural history. Payers then balk at million-dollar prices built on thin evidence, and post-market withdrawals become more likely when real-world data disappoints.
current_state: Regulators accept small trials for ultra-rare diseases out of necessity, but the evidence gap fuels reimbursement refusals and post-market withdrawals. Better trial designs for tiny populations remain an unsolved methodological problem.

sources.title: Challenges for gene therapy in the financial sustainability of health systems

title: Gene therapy trials too small to prove durability
why_it_blocks: Thin evidence supports neither confident prescribing nor sustainable pricing. The trial-design trap — too few patients for robust science — undermines the very therapies it is meant to validate, eroding trust with each uncertain approval.
